commonMistakes: Mixing raw values and matchers in one call, which throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
Mocking the class under test instead of its collaborators.
Verifying every internal call, making tests brittle.
detailedAnswer: A mock is a Mockito object with no real behaviour: you stub its answers with when(...).thenReturn(...) and optionally verify interactions with verify(...). A stub, in the strict vocabulary, returns canned answers without verification (in everyday Mockito usage, 'stubbing' just means programming a mock). A fake is a small real implementation, such as an in-memory repository backed by a HashMap, with genuine behaviour. A spy wraps a real object: real methods run unless you stub them. Choose a mock to verify a call or simulate a failure cheaply, a fake when simple stateful behaviour is worth reusing across tests, and a spy sparingly, when you cannot easily refactor to a seam.
followUps: When would you choose a fake over a mock?
Why is over-verifying interactions harmful?
question: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, a fake, and a spy?
shortAnswer: A mock is a Mockito object with no real behaviour, used for stubbing and verification; a stub returns canned answers; a fake is a small real implementation; a spy wraps a real object and runs real methods unless stubbed.
tips: Give one concrete example of each, not just definitions.
Mention the fake example: an in-memory repository.
title: Mock vs stub vs fake vs spy

commonMistakes: Using when(...) on a void method, which cannot work because the call returns nothing.
Forgetting the doX().when(...) form for doNothing and doAnswer as well as doThrow.
detailedAnswer: when(mock.voidMethod()) cannot work: Java evaluates the void call before Mockito sees it, and there is no return value for when to receive. The reverse form solves this: doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(mock).voidMethod(args), and likewise doNothing().when(...) and doAnswer(...).when(...) for void methods. The same form is also needed when stubbing a method on a spy, because when(spy.method()) would execute the real method during stubbing.
followUps: Why is the doX().when(...) form also needed for spies?
How would you stub a void method to do nothing?
question: How do you stub a void method in Mockito to throw an exception, and why can you not use when() for it?
shortAnswer: Use doThrow(...).when(mock).voidMethod(args), because when() cannot wrap a void call: the call returns nothing for when to receive.
tips: State the Java evaluation reason, not just the syntax.
Mention that the same form applies to spies.
title: Stubbing void methods in Mockito

commonMistakes: Saying matchers are a style preference rather than a mechanism with a stack.
Wrapping only some arguments in matchers and leaving others raw.
detailedAnswer: Mockito records argument matchers on an internal stack as they are evaluated during the stub or verify call. A raw value leaves no matcher on the stack, so Mockito cannot align the arguments with the matchers and throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime. The fix is to wrap every argument in a matcher: when(repo.find(anyString(), eq(10))). This applies equally to stubbing with when and to verification with verify.
followUps: What exception is thrown, and when: compile time or runtime?
How do you match an argument with a custom predicate?
question: Why can you not mix raw values and argument matchers in a single Mockito call?
shortAnswer: Mockito records matchers on a stack as they are evaluated; a raw value leaves no matcher, so arguments cannot be aligned and Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
tips: Name the exception and that it is a runtime failure.
Show the fix: wrap every argument, e.g. eq(10).
title: Mockito matcher mixing rule

commonMistakes: Only testing happy paths and missing boundaries, nulls, and empty inputs.
Testing every private helper, coupling the suite to implementation details.
detailedAnswer: Good tests are FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, and Timely, plus readable and resilient to harmless refactoring. Design them around the public contract: group inputs into equivalence classes (sets expected to behave the same way), test one member of each, and add the boundary values between classes, where off-by-one errors cluster. For a percent valid in 0-100, that means -1 and 101 (invalid), 0 and 100 (boundaries), and a middle value. Name tests after behaviour and condition so failures are self-explanatory.
followUps: How do you choose inputs when you cannot test them all?
When is it acceptable to test a private method?
question: How do you design a good unit test, and how do you choose which inputs to test?
shortAnswer: Test the public contract with FIRST qualities: fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating, timely. Choose inputs by equivalence classes plus boundary values, where bugs cluster.
tips: Use the 0-100 percent example with -1, 0, 100, 101.
Mention that private-method testing is a sign the code should be extracted.
title: Test design and boundary values

commonMistakes: Saying the pyramid is about test count alone, ignoring cost and failure precision.
Recommending end-to-end tests for everything because they are most realistic.
detailedAnswer: Cost and speed increase up the pyramid while failure precision decreases: a unit test failure names the broken unit, while an end-to-end failure only says something in a whole flow broke. So most coverage belongs in cheap, precise unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle catch wiring and contract mistakes, and a few end-to-end tests at the top cover critical user journeys. A suite dominated by end-to-end tests is the ice-cream cone anti-pattern: slow, hard to debug, and eventually not run.
followUps: What is the ice-cream cone anti-pattern?
When is an end-to-end test worth its cost?
question: Why is the test pyramid shaped the way it is?
shortAnswer: Cost and speed rise up the pyramid while failure precision falls, so most coverage belongs in cheap, precise unit tests, with fewer integration and end-to-end tests above them.
tips: Name the ice-cream cone anti-pattern unprompted.
Tie each layer to what it catches that the layer below cannot.
title: Test pyramid rationale

commonMistakes: Saying 'just re-run it' instead of diagnosing the cause.
Deleting a flaky test and silently losing its coverage.
detailedAnswer: A flaky test passes and fails without code changes, usually from shared mutable state, time dependence, un-awaited async work, randomness, or ordering assumptions. Each has a concrete cure: reset state in @BeforeEach and never rely on test order; inject a Clock and use Clock.fixed for time; await async conditions with a timeout instead of a guessed Thread.sleep; seed random generators and sort before asserting; mock or fake real network and file-system dependencies in unit tests. The process is quarantine the test so it does not block the suite, reproduce it, fix the root cause, and only then un-quarantine it.
followUps: What is the injected-Clock example for time-dependent flakiness?
When is quarantining better than deleting a flaky test?
question: What causes a flaky test, and how do you fix one?
shortAnswer: Shared state, time dependence, un-awaited async work, randomness, and ordering assumptions. Fix the root cause (injected Clock, awaited conditions, reset state), quarantine until fixed, and never just re-run or delete.
tips: Name at least two causes with their specific cures.
Use the Clock.fixed example; interviewers ask for it.
title: Flaky tests: causes and cures

commonMistakes: Reciting TDD as a universal rule without its costs.
Confusing TDD with simply writing tests after the code.
detailedAnswer: TDD is the Red-Green-Refactor rhythm: write a failing test for the next behaviour, write the smallest code that passes, then refactor with the test as a safety net. Its real benefit is design pressure: code written to be testable tends to have small classes, explicit dependencies, and clear boundaries. Its costs are discipline and a slower first pass, and it fits poorly for exploratory work where the behaviour is not yet understood, since the test cannot be written before the behaviour is known. A balanced answer names both sides.
followUps: What design pressure does TDD create?
When would you not use TDD?
question: What is TDD, and when is it a good or poor fit?
shortAnswer: TDD is Red-Green-Refactor: failing test, minimal passing code, refactor. It drives testable design, but costs discipline and fits poorly when behaviour is still being discovered.
tips: Be honest about both benefit and cost.
Mention design pressure: small classes, explicit dependencies.
title: Test-driven development trade-offs

commonMistakes: Using @MockBean in new Spring Boot 3.4+ code, where it is deprecated.
Using @MockitoBean in a plain unit test, where there is no context.
detailedAnswer: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer: controllers, filters, converters, and MVC infrastructure. Services and repositories are not loaded, so you replace them with @MockitoBean and test through MockMvc without starting a server. @SpringBootTest loads the full application context and is for behaviour that is the wiring itself. @MockitoBean is the Spring Boot 3.4+ replacement for the deprecated @MockBean, from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito; it only makes sense where a context exists, so plain unit tests use @Mock instead.
followUps: Why can overusing @MockitoBean slow a suite?
What does @DataJpaTest load instead?
question: What does @WebMvcTest load, how does it differ from @SpringBootTest, and where does @MockitoBean fit?
shortAnswer: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, with services replaced by @MockitoBean and tested via MockMvc; @SpringBootTest loads the full context. @MockitoBean is the Spring Boot 3.4+ replacement for deprecated @MockBean.
tips: Name the 3.4+ change and the new import package.
Mention context caching as the cost of overusing @MockitoBean.
title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest and @MockitoBean

commonMistakes: Assuming @DataJpaTest uses the production database by default.
Testing a repository with a mocked repository, which verifies nothing about the query.
detailedAnswer: @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer: entities, repositories, and an embedded database by default, with each test running in a transaction that is rolled back afterwards so tests do not pollute each other. That rollback is what makes repository tests independent without manual cleanup. It is the right layer for verifying that a derived query method actually works, because a unit test with a mocked repository could never catch a misspelled query name. If the test must run against a real database, add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) and supply the datasource, for example from Testcontainers.
followUps: How do you make a @DataJpaTest run against Testcontainers PostgreSQL?
Why is rollback a problem for testing commit side effects?
question: What does @DataJpaTest load, and why is it transactional with rollback?
shortAnswer: @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer against an embedded database, in a transaction rolled back afterwards, so repository tests stay independent and verify real query behaviour.
tips: Contrast with a mocked repository, which cannot catch a bad query.
Mention Replace.NONE as the bridge to Testcontainers.
title: @DataJpaTest and transactional rollback

commonMistakes: Forgetting Replace.NONE, so the test silently runs on the embedded database.
Hardcoding the internal port 5432 instead of using the mapped port.
detailedAnswer: Testcontainers starts real services in Docker containers for tests and removes them afterwards. In Spring Boot 3.1+, @ServiceConnection on a @Container field wires the container's connection details into the application context automatically, replacing hand-written @DynamicPropertySource registration for standard cases. Two details are essential: Docker maps the container's internal port to a random host port, so you must use the mapped port (or let @ServiceConnection handle it), and @DataJpaTest substitutes an embedded database by default, so you must add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) or the container is never actually used.
followUps: What happens if Docker is not available where tests run?
Why pin image tags to a major version instead of latest?
question: How do Testcontainers and Spring Boot connect, and what are the two details that most often go wrong?
shortAnswer: @ServiceConnection (Spring Boot 3.1+) wires a container's connection details into the context automatically. The common mistakes are hardcoding the internal port instead of the mapped port, and forgetting Replace.NONE so @DataJpaTest silently uses an embedded database.
tips: Name both failure modes explicitly.
Mention that @DynamicPropertySource is the older, still-valid alternative.
title: Testcontainers with Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Putting every test in a container and losing the pyramid's speed benefit.
Using a shared dev database for tests, which reintroduces interference.
detailedAnswer: An embedded database such as H2 has a different SQL dialect and feature set from production PostgreSQL, so it tolerates queries production would reject and hides real failures. Testcontainers runs the actual production database in a disposable container, giving real fidelity with test isolation: each test class gets a fresh database, so tests cannot pollute each other. The price is Docker availability, slower startup, and more moving parts, so container tests belong in the integration layer and should be few and focused on database-specific behaviour. A shared dev or staging database is the option to avoid: tests interfere with each other and with developers.
followUps: When is an embedded database good enough?
How do you handle container tests in CI?
question: Why use Testcontainers instead of an embedded database, and when should you not use it?
shortAnswer: Testcontainers runs the real production database in a disposable container, catching dialect and feature differences an embedded database hides. Its cost (Docker, startup time) means it belongs only in focused integration tests.
tips: Give the H2-versus-PostgreSQL dialect example.
Name the shared-database anti-pattern as what not to do.
title: When Testcontainers is worth its cost

commonMistakes: Answering only about context caching, or only about test choice, without connecting them.
Recommending @SpringBootTest for everything because it is most faithful.
detailedAnswer: Choosing the smallest context that can catch the bug keeps the suite fast: unit tests for logic, slices for one layer, full context only for wiring. Context caching makes this concrete: Spring reuses a context across tests with identical configuration, but replacing different beans with @MockitoBean changes the context definition and forces expensive rebuilds, so overusing it across many test classes slows the suite even when each individual test is a slice test. The design rule that follows is to push logic down to plain unit tests, use @MockitoBean only at the boundary of a slice test, and keep full-context tests few.
followUps: How does Spring decide whether a context can be reused?
What test-only configuration alternatives avoid @MockitoBean?
question: How do test-layer choice and Spring context caching interact to determine suite speed?
shortAnswer: Spring caches contexts with identical configuration; differing @MockitoBean replacements force expensive rebuilds. So push logic to unit tests, use @MockitoBean only at slice boundaries, and keep full-context tests few.
tips: Connect the caching mechanism to the practical rule.
Mention @TestConfiguration as an alternative for test-only beans with real behaviour.
title: Context caching and suite speed
